The Luddites were 19th-century English textile workers (or self-employed weavers who feared the end of their trade) who protested against newly developed labour-economizing technologies, primarily between 1811 and 1816.

The Attack:

In 1812, Luddites in Yorkshire decide to attack a large mill near Leeds (they had already attacked or intimated smaller mills in the area). There were two substantial mills who had defied the Luddites. William Horsfall near Huddlesfield, who had a cannon mounted in his mill, and the quiet but determined William Cartwright of Rawfolds.

According to tradition, the Luddites drew lots to decide which mill should be their first objective. The choice fell on Rawfolds. The attack upon Rawfolds has become legendary. Perhaps 150 Luddites took part. Led by George Mellor, a young cropper from a small finishing shop at Longroyd Bridge near Huddersfield, the Luddites exchanged a birsk fire with the embattled defenders for twenty minutes. Under cover of this fire, a small party of hammermen and men with hatchets made repeated attempts to break down the heavy doors of the mill. This party suffered serious casualties, at least five being wounded, two of whom – mortally wounded – were left behind when the Luddites suddenly retreated. It is said that their commander, Mellor, was the last to be left on the field, and that he could not help the wounded men since he was helping to carry another (his own cousin) to safety. The ground around the mill was littered with muskets, axes, pikes and metal implements.

The Aftermath:

The gunfire at Rawfolds signaled a profound emotional reconciliation between the large mill-owners and the authorities. Economic interest had triumphed, and the ultimate loyalty of the manufacturers when faced with working-class Jacobinism was displayed in one dramatic incident.

 

The folk-traditions of the Rawfolds attack emphasized the heroism of the Luddites and the callousness of the defenders. After the retreat, Cartwright was alleged to have refused water or aid to the two mortally wounded men, unless they divulged Luddite secrets. Hammond Roberson is supposed to have hung over the bedside of one of them, John Booth, the nineteen-year-old son on an Anglican clergyman, waiting for a dying confession. At the moment of death, young Booth signaled to Roberson – “Can you keep a secret?” “Yes, yes,” replied the eager Roberson, “I can.” “So can I,” replied Booth, and shortly after he died.

 

More than one of the small party of soldiers at Cartwright’s mill had shown a marked lack of enthusiasm for duty, and one of them refused to fire his musket during the entire twenty minutes of the affair, “because I might hit some of my brothers”. The unfortunate soldier (from the Cumberland Militia) was court martialed and sentenced to receive 300 lashes-a probable death sentence. The punishment was administered at Rawfolds, and Cartwright was able to regain a portion of public favour by securing the remission of the greater part of the sentence. He regained little. In popular forklore, Cartwright and Roberson were simply the “bloodhounds”. For months, despite the presence of 4,000 troops in the West Riding and the widespread employment of spies, not one of the Rawfolds attackers was clearly identified. Traditions speak of…surgeons who refused to pass on information.

 

The crises…cemented popular feeling against the magistrates and the large employers alike.

Sources: Thompson, E.P., The making of the English working class (p. 559-564). Vintage Books

This forum is privately owned.

From the User Agreement:

Subverses may create their own rules and enforce them as they see fit, providing they do not violate the terms of this agreement.

There not only is nothing in that agreement to prohibit deletions for any reason - it explicitly states elsewhere in the User Agreement:

Without advance notice and at any time, we may, for violations of this agreement or for any other reason we choose: (1) suspend your access to voat, (2) suspend or terminate Your Account, and/or (3) remove any of your User Content from voat.

And that, as they say, is that. Mods may make whatever rules they want so long as they don't violate the user agreement and the user agreement allows for deletions "for any reason we choose." That is what the owners of the site have decreed, that is what the users of the site have agreed to, and that's just the way it is.

A separate post with my personal opinion (which I accept to be ultimately meaningless, since I do not own a share of this forum and thus have no authority over how it's run, which is something of which more people need to be aware):

The issue, really, is oddly similar to the overarching issue of property rights as it pertains to the real world. And curiously enough, much of Voat seems keen on what really is, at heart, a "communist" public property model. That's really what the position that the users should control the management of a sub comes down to - it's fundamentally identical to the communist position that the workers should own the means of production. In fact, it's not only the same ultimate position - it's even generally supported by the same fundamental reasoning - that the users are the ones who make a sub what it is, while the "owner" is just the person who created it in the first place, so the users should have control and the "owner" should be shut out.

I'm sure that some number of goats don't want to face the realization that they're advocating a "communist" public property model here, but that is in fact what they're doing.

The alternative, as in the real world, is a "capitalist" private property model. And under such a model, the "owner" of a given sub - who is, according to the rules put in place by the owners of the site, the creator of the sub or the person to whom that ownership has been duly transferred, has full rights to do with the sub as they please, including putting whatever rules they might wish in place and enforcing them however they might please. And that's just the way it is. If one is going to have a private property model, then the owners MUST possess the authority to do as they please with their property.

Personally, I prefer a private property model, since that's been shown to bring better results over the long term. And yes - the trade-off for a private property model is that the owners must possess the authority to do as they please with their property. Anyone who is dissatisfied with the way in which an owner manages his property is perfectly free to take his business elsewhere, and allowed to do so, the market will determine which subs will be rewarded with content and which subs will not be accordingly.
